title: The Girl Who Smelled Like Soup

pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 3. Bowls sold: 71. Weather: drizzle. Times Lin washed her hair: 3.*

Class five-two smelled of dry chalk and wet wool. Ms. Wu was writing fractions on the blackboard, her pencil moving in quick, angry scribbles. I sat between Hui-Ting, who was tall enough to touch the ceiling tiles with her braids, and the window. The window was a bad choice. It let in the cold and the smell of the street.

Jun leaned over from the next row. He had spiky hair that stood up like a startled hedgehog and a grin that never left his face. He sniffed the air near my elbow. Then he sniffed again, louder.

"Chen Yun-Lin smells like beef noodles," he announced to the class.

Half the room laughed. The other half tried not to. I pulled my sleeve to my nose. It smelled of soy sauce and star anise. My face went hot, the kind of heat that starts in the ears and moves to the forehead. I did not say anything. I just looked at my shoes and counted the holes in the rubber soles. One, two, three.
pages.image: A classroom scene with a spiky-haired boy leaning over to sniff a girl's elbow while she sits stiffly with a red face, surrounded by laughing classmates and a teacher writing on a chalkboard.

pages.text:
That night, I decided the problem was the shampoo, or perhaps a serious lack of it. I reached for Ma’s lavender bottle, the expensive one with the pump top, and washed my hair once. Then twice. I washed it a third time because my scalp felt like it was still wearing a hat.

The bathroom filled with a mist that smelled like a flower shop losing an argument with a soup pot. It was a confusing scent, neither clean nor beef, just heavy, purple lavender hanging in the air.

Ma leaned against the doorframe, her glasses sliding down her nose while a clip held back her dark hair. She looked at the steam, then at me.

"Star anise is not a shame," she said quietly.

She did not wait for an answer. Instead, she closed the door gently, though I heard her footsteps retreating down the hall. I looked in the mirror. My hair was clean. It still smelled like home.
pages.image: A bathroom mirror reflecting a girl with wet, clean hair looking tired, with a background of swirling steam and a bottle of lavender shampoo on the sink counter.

pages.text:
The next day, a new girl sat in my row. Her name was Yi-Chen. She wore a pink puffy vest that looked brand new and shoes so clean they reflected the fluorescent lights. She had come from Taipei, she said. She lived near where the new mall was going up.

"Is it true," she asked, looking around the classroom with wide eyes, "that you eat food from carts? With plastic stools?"

I nodded.

Yi-Chen frowned. "That sounds so old-fashioned," she said. "In Taipei, everything is clean and digital. You order on a screen. You don't have to talk to the cook."

I opened my mouth. I had a whole sentence ready. It involved the taste of the broth and the way the steam rises. I wanted to say it was warm. I wanted to say it was real.

Instead, I closed my mouth.

"Oh," I said.

It was a very small sound. It felt like a pebble dropped into a deep well.
pages.image: A girl in a bright pink puffy vest looking down at a classmate with a skeptical expression, sitting at a desk in a modern classroom with bright overhead lighting.

pages.text:
After school, the lane was already waking up. Plastic stools stood stacked in the aisles, and the canvas tarps were being unrolled with a heavy, rustling sound. I walked to stall number nineteen, but this time I did not look at the steaming pot. I looked at it with Yi-Chen’s eyes.

The rims of the bowls were chipped. The wooden tables were scratched deep enough to catch chopsticks, and the air felt thick with smoke and the sharp, greasy tang of frying oil. It was messy. It was loud. It was definitely not clean.

I pulled my notebook from my bag and uncapped my pencil. I began to draw a sleek white counter, the kind you see in those glossy magazines, followed by a large screen where the menu would appear. Then I sketched a machine that dispensed little numbered tickets. It looked perfect. It looked modern. It was exactly what Yi-Chen would like, and a part of me wanted to believe it, too.

Ama shuffled past, carrying a stack of bowls that wobbled dangerously high. She saw the notebook and I quickly turned the page to a blank sheet, my heart giving a small, guilty hop. She did not ask. She just set the bowls down with a clatter and went to the pot.
pages.image: A girl sketching a modern, sleek food counter and digital screen in a notebook, sitting at a rough wooden table in a busy market setting with steam rising in the background.

pages.text:
Ama stood by the large pot, her hands moving in a steady rhythm. She was humming. It was the same song she always hummed, one with no words that went up and down like the steam rising and falling.

I looked at my drawing of the white counter and the digital screen. Then I looked at Ama’s hands. They were stained with soy sauce. They were strong. They were the reason the soup tasted right.

My song. My drawing. My modern idea.

I could not draw the song. I could not measure the steam. I could not put the way she hummed into a white counter.

I tore the page out of my notebook. I folded it into a small, tight square. I put it in my jacket pocket. It stayed there for weeks. I did not pull it out. I just felt it there, like a secret I was keeping from myself.
pages.image: A grandmother with short silver curls and a floral vest standing by a large steaming pot, while a girl in a green jacket looks down at a crumpled piece of paper in her hand.
